council.name: Norwich City Council
council.remit_note: Norwich City Council is a district council with city status. In Norfolk, local government is split between two councils, and Norwich does the half you meet day to day: the council housing it owns and manages itself, bin collections, parks, planning applications, and licensing — who may sell alcohol, put on entertainment, or serve hot food and drink late at night. Roads and potholes, schools and libraries, and social care for children and adults belong to Norfolk County Council instead, so you will not find those here.

composition.summary: Norwich City Council has 39 councillors: three for each of the city's 13 wards. The Green Party holds 21 of those seats, Labour 12, the Liberal Democrats 3, Reform UK 2, and one councillor sits as an independent. The council's own leader and cabinet page shows that the leader of the council and all seven cabinet members are Green Party councillors.

gaps.description: The council does not publish the date of its next election anywhere we could find, so this page does not give one.

Norwich does not publish councillors' own websites or social media accounts anywhere on its councillor pages, so there are none to record. This project would only ever list such an address as the council printed it, and would never open it.

The council prints a personal mobile number for many councillors. Neither this page nor the archive behind it carries one. The numbers are removed from every file when it is downloaded, before anything is saved, so what is stored here reads '[phone number removed]'. That makes this archive not quite a byte-for-byte copy of what the council published, and the same rule takes out the council's own switchboard numbers where they appear on these pages. Anyone who needs a number can find it on the council's own page, which is linked.

For elections before 2023 the council's results archive no longer carries a page, so the dates come from the committee system's own election history and no vote count or majority is shown. In wards electing more than one councillor at the same time — Wensum in 2026 — each winner's majority is worked out against the same best-placed losing candidate, so two winners in one ward can show different majorities.

The 2025 result for Bowthorpe gives Richard Lawes a majority of one vote. The arithmetic follows from the council's own table, but that table prints no vote count at all for one of the candidates, so the figure cannot be checked against the source and is flagged for a person to confirm.

The council published turnout for each ward in 2023 but not in 2024, 2025 or 2026, so turnout is missing for the more recent elections. Majorities are worked out from the council's own vote counts: the winner's votes minus the best-placed candidate who did not win a seat.

Norwich publishes 22 of its 39 registers of interests as scanned pictures of a paper form, with no text in the file. A scan can be looked at but not read by a computer, searched, or quoted, so nothing from those 22 is shown here. Each councillor's page links their own form so you can read it yourself.

Norwich uses two versions of its register form and they behave differently. Six of the 17 readable registers are on the February 2016 form, which has a single column headed 'Details of member's interests'; everything on those is shown. The other 11 are on the April 2026 form, which puts a councillor's own answers beside their partner's in the pecuniary table, and the two columns run together when the file is read as text. On those 11, a pecuniary row that lists more than one answer is left out rather than risk printing a partner's job under a councillor's name. The 'other registrable interests' box on both forms is a single list with no partner column, so it is always shown in full. Each councillor's own note says which form theirs is and what, if anything, is missing.

The council does not publish a councillor's register at an ordinary web address. Each one sits behind a button on that councillor's page, which redirects to a signed address that then serves the file to anyone. Those addresses were resolved by hand, once, on 8 September 2026. The 17 readable ones were fetched and checked; the 22 scanned ones were not fetched, so their links are recorded as resolved but have not been opened by this project.

Attendance is counted over a rolling twelve months ending on the day the council's page was read, not over a council year or a financial year. Two councillors' figures are therefore comparable with each other but not with any figure the council publishes for a fixed period.

The council's allowances schedule has four money columns — basic allowance, special responsibility, expenses and total — but prints a figure in only three of them for almost everyone. Read as text, there is no way to tell whether the middle figure is a special responsibility allowance or expenses. This page therefore shows the basic allowance and the total, which are unambiguous, and says nothing about special responsibility for anyone.

The most recent allowances the council has published are for 2024-25, so councillors elected in May 2025 or May 2026 are not in that schedule and no figure is shown for them. The schedule gives a surname and an initial rather than a full name, so a figure is shown only where exactly one councillor matches it and the council's record has them in office during that year. Where someone served part of the year the figures are for that part, which is why some are much smaller than others.

The council explains most of its committees in plain English, but publishes no such description for the audit committee or the treasury management committee. Their terms of reference are in the constitution, which is not part of this archive.

The council's committee index also lists an informal planning applications briefing and a retired Norwich Highways Agency committee. Neither has a membership on any councillor's page, so neither has an entry here.
Norwich's pay policy statement says the council must have a Section 151 officer — the person legally responsible for its money — but does not say which post or which person holds the role.

The council's page about its officers names the chief executive and the executive directors but not the holder of the monitoring officer post, so this page does not name them either. Officer pay is published as a band for the grade, not as what an individual is paid, and no council document links a named officer to a band — that join is ours, made from the officers page for the name and the salaries list for the band.
